title: Finding the Area of a Region Bounded by Functions That Cross
snippet: Finding the Area of a Region Bounded by Functions That Cross: If R is the region between the graphs of the functions f(x) = \sin x and g(x) = \cos x over the interval \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack, find the area of region R. The...
body_xml: If R is the region between the graphs of the functions $$f(x) = \sin x$$ and $$g(x) = \cos x$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack,$$ find the area of region $$R.$$ The region is depicted in the following figure. The graphs of the functions intersect at $$x = {\pi/4}.$$ For $$x \in \left\lbrack {0,{\pi/4}} \right\rbrack,$$ $$\cos x \geq \sin x,$$ so $$\left| {f(x) - g(x)} \right| = \left| {\sin x - \cos x} \right| = \cos x - \sin x.$$ On the other hand, for $$x \in \left\lbrack {{\pi/4},\pi} \right\rbrack,$$ $$\sin x \geq \cos x,$$ so $$\left| {f(x) - g(x)} \right| = \left| {\sin x - \cos x} \right| = \sin x - \cos x.$$ Then $$\begin{array}{cl} A & {= \int_{a}^{b}\left| {f(x) - g(x)} \right|dx} \\ & {= \int_{0}^{\pi}\left| {\sin x - \cos x} \right|dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/4}\left( {\cos x - \sin x} \right)dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}\left( {\sin x - \cos x} \right)dx} \\ & {= \left. \left\lbrack {\sin x + \cos x} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{\pi/4} + \left. \left\lbrack {-\cos x - \sin x} \right\rbrack \right|_{\pi/4}^{\pi}} \\ & {= \left( {\sqrt{2} - 1} \right) + \left( {1 + \sqrt{2}} \right) = 2\sqrt{2}.} \end{array}$$ The area of the region is $$2\sqrt{2}$$ units2.

title: Finding the Area of a Complex Region
snippet: Finding the Area of a Complex Region: Consider the region depicted in Figure 2.7. Find the area of R. As with Example 2.3, we need to divide the interval into two pieces. The graphs of the functions intersect at x = 1 (set f(x) = g(x) and...
body_xml: Consider the region depicted in Figure 2.7. Find the area of $$R.$$ As with Example 2.3, we need to divide the interval into two pieces. The graphs of the functions intersect at $$x = 1$$ (set $$f(x) = g(x)$$ and solve for x), so we evaluate two separate integrals: one over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ and one over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,2} \right\rbrack.$$ Over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack,$$ the region is bounded above by $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and below by the x-axis, so we have $$A_{1} = \int_{0}^{1}x^{2}dx = \left. \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right|_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}.$$ Over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,2} \right\rbrack,$$ the region is bounded above by $$g(x) = 2 - x$$ and below by the $$x \text{-axis,}$$ so we have $$A_{2} = \int_{1}^{2}\left( {2 - x} \right)dx = \left. \left\lbrack {2x - \frac{x^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}.$$ Adding these areas together, we obtain $$A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{6}.$$ The area of the region is $$5/6$$ units2.

title: Integrating with Respect to y
snippet: Integrating with Respect to y: Let’s revisit Example 2.4, only this time let’s integrate with respect to y. Let R be the region depicted in Figure 2.10. Find the area of R by integrating with respect to y. We must first express the graphs...
body_xml: Let’s revisit Example 2.4, only this time let’s integrate with respect to $$y.$$ Let $$R$$ be the region depicted in Figure 2.10. Find the area of $$R$$ by integrating with respect to $$y.$$ We must first express the graphs as functions of $$y.$$ As we saw at the beginning of this section, the curve on the left can be represented by the function $$x = v(y) = \sqrt{y},$$ and the curve on the right can be represented by the function $$x = u(y) = 2 - y.$$ Now we have to determine the limits of integration. The region is bounded below by the x-axis, so the lower limit of integration is $$y = 0.$$ The upper limit of integration is determined by the point where the two graphs intersect, which is the point $$\left( {1,1} \right),$$ so the upper limit of integration is $$y = 1.$$ Thus, we have $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ Calculating the area of the region, we get $$\begin{array}{cl} A & {= \int_{c}^{d}\left\lbrack {u(y) - v(y)} \right\rbrack dy} \\ & {= \int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\left( {2 - y} \right) - \sqrt{y}} \right\rbrack dy = \left. \left\lbrack {2y - \frac{y^{2}}{2} - \frac{2}{3}y^{3/2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{1}} \\ & {= \frac{5}{6}.} \end{array}$$ The area of the region is $$5/6$$ units2.

title: Deriving the Formula for the Volume of a Pyramid
snippet: Deriving the Formula for the Volume of a Pyramid: We know from geometry that the formula for the volume of a pyramid is V = \frac{1}{3}Ah. If the pyramid has a square base, this becomes V = \frac{1}{3}a^{2}h, where a denotes the length of...
body_xml: We know from geometry that the formula for the volume of a pyramid is $$V = \frac{1}{3}Ah.$$ If the pyramid has a square base, this becomes $$V = \frac{1}{3}a^{2}h,$$ where $$a$$ denotes the length of one side of the base. We are going to use the slicing method to derive this formula. We want to apply the slicing method to a pyramid with a square base. To set up the integral, consider the pyramid shown in Figure 2.14, oriented along the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ We first want to determine the shape of a cross-section of the pyramid. We know the base is a square, so the cross-sections are squares as well (step 1). Now we want to determine a formula for the area of one of these cross-sectional squares. Looking at Figure 2.14(b), and using a proportion, since these are similar triangles, we have $$\frac{s}{a} = \frac{x}{h} \text{or} s = \frac{ax}{h}.$$ Therefore, the area of one of the cross-sectional squares is $$A(x) = s^{2} = \left( \frac{ax}{h} \right)^{2}\left( { \text{step} 2} \right).$$ Then we find the volume of the pyramid by integrating from $$0 \text{to} h$$ (step $$3):$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int\limits_{0}^{h}{A(x)}}dx} \\ & {= {\int\limits_{0}^{h}\left( \frac{ax}{h} \right)^{2}}dx = \frac{a^{2}}{h^{2}}{\int\limits_{0}^{h}x^{2}}dx} \\ & {= \left. \left\lbrack {\frac{a^{2}}{h^{2}}\left( {\frac{1}{3}x^{3}} \right)} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{h} = \frac{1}{3}a^{2}h.} \end{array}$$ This is the formula we were looking for.

snippet: Using the Slicing Method to find the Volume of a Solid of Revolution: Use the slicing method to find the volume of the solid of revolution bounded by the graphs of f(x) = x^{2} - 4x + 5,x = 1, \text{and} x = 4, and rotated about the x...
body_xml: Use the slicing method to find the volume of the solid of revolution bounded by the graphs of $$f(x) = x^{2} - 4x + 5,x = 1, \text{and} x = 4,$$ and rotated about the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ Using the problem-solving strategy, we first sketch the graph of the quadratic function over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ as shown in the following figure. Next, revolve the region around the x-axis, as shown in the following figure. Since the solid was formed by revolving the region around the $$x \text{-axis,}$$ the cross-sections are circles (step 1). The area of the cross-section, then, is the area of a circle, and the radius of the circle is given by $$f(x).$$ Use the formula for the area of the circle: $$A(x) = \pi r^{2} = \pi\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2} = \pi\left( {x^{2} - 4x + 5} \right)^{2} \text{(step 2)} .$$ The volume, then, is (step 3) $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int\limits_{a}^{b}{A(x)}}dx} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{\pi\left( {x^{2} - 4x + 5} \right)^{2}}}dx = \pi{\int_{1}^{4}\left( {x^{4} - 8x^{3} + 26x^{2} - 40x + 25} \right)}dx} \\ & {= \left. {\pi\left( {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - 2x^{4} + \frac{26x^{3}}{3} - 20x^{2} + 25x} \right)} \right|_{1}^{4} = \frac{78}{5}\pi.} \end{array}$$ The volume is $$78\pi/5.$$

We have $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int_{a}^{b}{\pi\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{\pi\left\lbrack \sqrt{x} \right\rbrack^{2}}}dx = \pi{\int_{1}^{4}{x dx}}} \\ & {= \left. {\frac{\pi}{2}x^{2}} \right|_{1}^{4} = \frac{15\pi}{2}.} \end{array}$$ The volume is $$\left( {15\pi} \right)/2$$ units3.

body_xml: Let $$R$$ be the region bounded by the graph of $$g(y) = \sqrt{4 - y}$$ and the $$y \text{-axis}$$ over the $$y \text{-axis}$$ interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack.$$ Use the disk method to find the volume of the solid of revolution generated by rotating $$R$$ around the $$y \text{-axis} .$$ Figure 2.20 shows the function and a representative disk that can be used to estimate the volume. Notice that since we are revolving the function around the $$y \text{-axis,}$$ the disks are horizontal, rather than vertical. The region to be revolved and the full solid of revolution are depicted in the following figure. To find the volume, we integrate with respect to $$y.$$ We obtain $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int_{c}^{d}\pi}\left\lbrack {g(y)} \right\rbrack^{2}dy} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}\pi}\left\lbrack \sqrt{4 - y} \right\rbrack^{2}dy = \pi{\int_{0}^{4}\left( {4 - y} \right)}dy} \\ & {= \left. {\pi\left\lbrack {4y - \frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack} \right|_{0}^{4} = 8\pi.} \end{array}$$ The volume is $$8\pi$$ units3.

body_xml: Find the volume of a solid of revolution formed by revolving the region bounded above by $$f(x) = 4 - x$$ and below by the $$x \text{-axis}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ around the line $$y = -2.$$ The graph of the region and the solid of revolution are shown in the following figure. We can’t apply the volume formula to this problem directly because the axis of revolution is not one of the coordinate axes. However, we still know that the area of the cross-section is the area of the outer circle less the area of the inner circle. Looking at the graph of the function, we see the radius of the outer circle is given by $$f(x) + 2,$$ which simplifies to $$f(x) + 2 = \left( {4 - x} \right) + 2 = 6 - x.$$ The radius of the inner circle is $$g(x) = 2.$$ Therefore, we have $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\pi\left\lbrack {\left( {6 - x} \right)^{2} - (2)^{2}} \right\rbrack}}dx} \\ & {= \pi{\int_{0}^{4}{\left( {x^{2} - 12x + 32} \right)dx}} = \left. {\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} - 6x^{2} + 32x} \right\rbrack} \right|_{0}^{4} = \frac{160\pi}{3} \text{units} ^{3}.} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Define $$R$$ as the region bounded above by the graph of the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ and below by the graph of the function $$g(x) = {1/x}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack.$$ Find the volume of the solid of revolution generated by revolving $$R$$ around the $$y \text{-axis} .$$ First, graph the region $$R$$ and the associated solid of revolution, as shown in the following figure. Note that the axis of revolution is the $$y \text{-axis} ,$$ so the radius of a shell is given simply by $$x.$$ We don’t need to make any adjustments to the x-term of our integrand. The height of a shell, though, is given by $$f(x) - g(x),$$ so in this case we need to adjust the $$f(x)$$ term of the integrand. Then the volume of the solid is given by $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int_{1}^{4}\left( {2\pi x\left( {f(x) - g(x)} \right)} \right)}dx} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {2\pi x\left( {\sqrt{x} - \frac{1}{x}} \right)} \right)dx}} = 2\pi{\int_{1}^{4}\left( {x^{3/2} - 1} \right)}dx} \\ & {= \left. {2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{2x^{5/2}}{5} - x} \right\rbrack} \right|_{1}^{4} = \frac{94\pi}{5} \text{units} ^{3}.} \end{array}$$

title: Selecting the Best Method
snippet: Selecting the Best Method: For each of the following problems, select the best method to find the volume of a solid of revolution generated by revolving the given region around the x \text{-axis} , and set up the integral to find the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.17" title="Selecting the Best Method">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following problems, select the best method to find the volume of a solid of revolution generated by revolving the given region around the $$x \text{-axis} ,$$ and set up the integral to find the volume (do not evaluate the integral).</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The region bounded by the graphs of $$y = x,$$ $$y = 2 - x,$$ and the $$x \text{-axis} .$$</item>
        <item>The region bounded by the graphs of $$y = 4x - x^{2}$$ and the $$x \text{-axis} .$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>First, sketch the region and the solid of revolution as shown. Figure 2.35 (a) The region $$R$$ bounded by two lines and the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ (b) The solid of revolution generated by revolving $$R$$ about the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ Looking at the region, if we want to integrate with respect to $$x,$$ we would have to break the integral into two pieces, because we have different functions bounding the region over $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack {1,2} \right\rbrack.$$ In this case, using the disk method, we would have $$V = {\int_{0}^{1}\left( {\pi x^{2}} \right)}dx + {\int_{1}^{2}\left( {\pi{(2 - x)}^{2}} \right)}dx.$$ If we used the shell method instead, we would use functions of $$y$$ to represent the curves, producing $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\left( {2\pi y\left\lbrack {\left( {2 - y} \right) - y} \right\rbrack} \right)}dy} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\left( {2\pi y\left\lbrack {2 - 2y} \right\rbrack} \right)}dy.} \end{array}$$ Neither of these integrals is particularly onerous, but since the shell method requires only one integral, and the integrand requires less simplification, we should probably go with the shell method in this case.</item>
        <item>First, sketch the region and the solid of revolution as shown. Figure 2.36 (a) The region $$R$$ between the curve and the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ (b) The solid of revolution generated by revolving $$R$$ about the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ Looking at the region, it would be problematic to define a horizontal rectangle; the region is bounded on the left and right by the same function. Therefore, we can dismiss the method of shells. The solid has no cavity in the middle, so we can use the method of disks. Then $$V = {\int_{0}^{4}\pi}\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{2}dx.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="2.18" title="Calculating the Arc Length of a Function of x">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3/2}.$$ Calculate the arc length of the graph of $$f(x)$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ Round the answer to three decimal places.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{1/2},$$ so $$\left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2} = 9x.$$ Then, the arc length is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Arc Length} & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} dx} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1 + 9x}} dx.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute $$u = 1 + 9x.$$ Then, $$du = 9 dx.$$ When $$x = 0,$$ then $$u = 1,$$ and when $$x = 1,$$ then $$u = 10.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Arc Length} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1 + 9x}} dx} \\ & {= \frac{1}{9}\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1 + 9x}9dx = \frac{1}{9}{\int_{1}^{10}\sqrt{u}} du} \\ & {= \left. {\frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}} \right|_{1}^{10} = \frac{2}{27}\left\lbrack {10\sqrt{10} - 1} \right\rbrack \approx 2.268 \text{units} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.19" title="Using a Computer or Calculator to Determine the Arc Length of a Function of x">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = x^{2}.$$ Calculate the arc length of the graph of $$f(x)$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,3} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have $$f^{\prime}(x) = 2x,$$ so $$\left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2} = 4x^{2}.$$ Then the arc length is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Arc Length} = {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} dx = {\int_{1}^{3}\sqrt{1 + 4x^{2}}} dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using a computer to approximate the value of this integral, we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{1}^{3}\sqrt{1 + 4x^{2}}} dx \approx 8.26815.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.6" title="Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution">
    <heading level="4">Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be a nonnegative smooth function over the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$ Then, the surface area of the surface of revolution formed by revolving the graph of $$f(x)$$ around the x-axis is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Surface Area} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {2\pi f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left( {f^{\prime}(x)} \right)^{2}}} \right)dx}}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Similarly, let $$g(y)$$ be a nonnegative smooth function over the interval $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack.$$ Then, the surface area of the surface of revolution formed by revolving the graph of $$g(y)$$ around the $$y \text{-axis}$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Surface Area} = {\int_{c}^{d}{\left( {2\pi g(y)\sqrt{1 + \left( {g^{\prime}(y)} \right)^{2}}} \right)dy}}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Calculating the Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution 1
snippet: Calculating the Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution 1: Let f(x) = \sqrt{x} over the interval \left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack. Find the surface area of the surface generated by revolving the graph of f(x) around the x \text{-axis} ....
body_xml: Let $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack.$$ Find the surface area of the surface generated by revolving the graph of $$f(x)$$ around the $$x \text{-axis} .$$ Round the answer to three decimal places. The graph of $$f(x)$$ and the surface of rotation are shown in the following figure. We have $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}.$$ Then, $$f^{\prime}(x) = {1/\left( {2\sqrt{x}} \right)}$$ and $$\left( {f^{\prime}(x)} \right)^{2} = {1/\left( {4x} \right)}.$$ Then, $$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Surface Area} & {= {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {2\pi f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left( {f^{\prime}(x)} \right)^{2}}} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}\left( {2\pi\sqrt{x}\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{4x}}} \right)}dx} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {2\pi\sqrt{x + \frac{1}{4}}} \right)dx}}.} \end{array}$$ Let $$u = x + {1/4}.$$ Then, $$du = dx.$$ When $$x = 1,$$ $$u = {5/4},$$ and when $$x = 4,$$ $$u = {17/4}.$$ This gives us $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {2\pi\sqrt{x + \frac{1}{4}}} \right)dx}} & {= {\int_{5/4}^{17/4}{2\pi\sqrt{u}}} du} \\ & {= 2\pi\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{5/4}^{17/4} = \frac{\pi}{6}\left\lbrack {17\sqrt{17} - 5\sqrt{5}} \right\rbrack \approx 30.846.} \end{array}$$

title: Calculating the Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution 2
snippet: Calculating the Surface Area of a Surface of Revolution 2: Let f(x) = y = \sqrt[3]{3x}. Consider the portion of the curve where 0 \leq y \leq 2. Find the surface area of the surface generated by revolving the graph of f(x) around the y...
body_xml: Let $$f(x) = y = \sqrt[3]{3x}.$$ Consider the portion of the curve where $$0 \leq y \leq 2.$$ Find the surface area of the surface generated by revolving the graph of $$f(x)$$ around the $$y \text{-axis} .$$ Notice that we are revolving the curve around the $$y \text{-axis} ,$$ and the interval is in terms of $$y,$$ so we want to rewrite the function as a function of y. We get $$x = g(y) = \left( {1/3} \right)y^{3}.$$ The graph of $$g(y)$$ and the surface of rotation are shown in the following figure. We have $$g(y) = \left( {1/3} \right)y^{3},$$ so $$g^{\prime}(y) = y^{2}$$ and $$\left( {g^{\prime}(y)} \right)^{2} = y^{4}.$$ Then $$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Surface Area} & {= {\int_{c}^{d}{\left( {2\pi g(y)\sqrt{1 + \left( {g^{\prime}(y)} \right)^{2}}} \right)dy}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2}\left( {2\pi\left( {\frac{1}{3}y^{3}} \right)\sqrt{1 + y^{4}}} \right)}dy} \\ & {= \frac{2\pi}{3}{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {y^{3}\sqrt{1 + y^{4}}} \right)}dy.} \end{array}$$ Let $$u = y^{4} + 1.$$ Then $$du = 4y^{3}dy.$$ When $$y = 0,$$ $$u = 1,$$ and when $$y = 2,$$ $$u = 17.$$ Then $$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{2\pi}{3}{\int_{0}^{2}\left( {y^{3}\sqrt{1 + y^{4}}} \right)}dy} & {= \frac{2\pi}{3}{\int_{1}^{17}{\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{u}du}}} \\ & {= \frac{\pi}{6}\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{1}^{17} = \frac{\pi}{9}\left\lbrack {(17)^{3/2} - 1} \right\rbrack \approx 24.118.} \end{array}$$

title: The Work Required to Stretch or Compress a Spring
snippet: The Work Required to Stretch or Compress a Spring: Suppose it takes a force of 10 N (in the negative direction) to compress a spring 0.2 m from the equilibrium position. How much work is done to stretch the spring 0.5 m from the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.25" title="The Work Required to Stretch or Compress a Spring">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose it takes a force of $$10$$ N (in the negative direction) to compress a spring $$0.2$$ m from the equilibrium position. How much work is done to stretch the spring $$0.5$$ m from the equilibrium position?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First find the spring constant, $$k.$$ When $$x = -0.2,$$ we know $$F(x) = -10,$$ so</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {F(x)} & = & {kx} \\ {- 10} & = & {k(-0.2)} \\ k & = & 50 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and $$F(x) = 50x.$$ Then, to calculate work, we integrate the force function, obtaining</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$W = {\int_{a}^{b}F}(x)dx = {\int_{0}^{0.5}5}0x dx = \left. {25x^{2}} \right|_{0}^{0.5} = 6.25.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The work done to stretch the spring is $$6.25$$ J.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: A Pumping Problem with a Noncylindrical Tank
snippet: A Pumping Problem with a Noncylindrical Tank: Assume a tank in the shape of an inverted cone, with height 12 ft and base radius 4 ft. The tank is full to start with, and water is pumped over the upper edge of the tank until the height of...
body_xml: Assume a tank in the shape of an inverted cone, with height $$12$$ ft and base radius $$4$$ ft. The tank is full to start with, and water is pumped over the upper edge of the tank until the height of the water remaining in the tank is $$4$$ ft. How much work is required to pump out that amount of water? The tank is depicted in Figure 2.54. As we did in the example with the cylindrical tank, we orient the $$x \text{-axis}$$ vertically, with the origin at the top of the tank and the downward direction being positive (step 1). The tank starts out full and ends with $$4$$ ft of water left, so, based on our chosen frame of reference, we need to partition the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,8} \right\rbrack.$$ Then, for $$i = 0,1,2 \text{,…} ,n,$$ let $$P = \left\{ x_{i} \right\}$$ be a regular partition of the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,8} \right\rbrack,$$ and for $$i = 1,2 \text{,…} ,n,$$ choose an arbitrary point $$x_{i}^{*} \in \left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack.$$ We can approximate the volume of a layer by using a disk, then use similar triangles to find the radius of the disk (see the following figure). From properties of similar triangles, we have $$\begin{array}{cll} \frac{r_{i}}{12 - x_{i}^{*}} & = & {\frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}} \\ {3r_{i}} & = & {12 - x_{i}^{*}} \\ r_{i} & = & \frac{12 - x_{i}^{*}}{3} \\ & = & {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}.} \end{array}$$ Then the volume of the disk is $$V_{i} = \pi\left( {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}} \right)^{2} \text{Δ} x \text{(step 2).}$$ The weight-density of water is $$62.4$$ lb/ft3, so the force needed to lift each layer is approximately $$F_{i} \approx 62.4\pi\left( {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}} \right)^{2} \text{Δ} x \text{(step 3).}$$ Based on the diagram, the distance the water must be lifted is approximately $$x_{i}^{*}$$ feet (step 4), so the approximate work needed to lift the layer is $$W_{i} \approx 62.4\pi x_{i}^{*}\left( {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}} \right)^{2} \text{Δ} x \text{(step 5).}$$ Summing the work required to lift all the layers, we get an approximate value of the total work: $$W = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}W_{i} \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}62.4\pi x_{i}^{*}\left( {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}} \right)^{2} \text{Δ} x \text{(step 6).}$$ Taking the limit as $$n\rightarrow\infty,$$ we obtain $$\begin{array}{cl} W & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}62.4\pi x_{i}^{*}\left( {4 - \frac{x_{i}^{*}}{3}} \right)^{2} \text{Δ} x} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{8}{62.4\pi x\left( {4 - \frac{x}{3}} \right)^{2}dx}}} \\ & {= 62.4\pi{\int_{0}^{8}{x\left( {16 - \frac{8x}{3} + \frac{x^{2}}{9}} \right)dx}} = 62.4\pi{\int_{0}^{8}{\left( {16x - \frac{8x^{2}}{3} + \frac{x^{3}}{9}} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= 62.4\pi\left. \left\lbrack {8x^{2} - \frac{8x^{3}}{9} + \frac{x^{4}}{36}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{8} = 10,649.6\pi \approx 33,456.7.} \end{array}$$ It takes approximately $$33,450$$ ft-lb of work to empty the tank to the desired level.

title: Finding Hydrostatic Force
snippet: Finding Hydrostatic Force: A water trough 15 ft long has ends shaped like inverted isosceles triangles, with base 8 ft and height 3 ft. Find the force on one end of the trough if the trough is full of water. Figure 2.58 shows the trough...
body_xml: A water trough 15 ft long has ends shaped like inverted isosceles triangles, with base 8 ft and height 3 ft. Find the force on one end of the trough if the trough is full of water. Figure 2.58 shows the trough and a more detailed view of one end. Select a frame of reference with the $$x \text{-axis}$$ oriented vertically and the downward direction being positive. Select the top of the trough as the point corresponding to $$x = 0$$ (step 1). The depth function, then, is $$s(x) = x.$$ Using similar triangles, we see that $$w(x) = 8 - \left( {8/3} \right)x$$ (step 2). Now, the weight density of water is $$62.4$$ lb/ft3 (step 3), so applying Equation 2.13, we obtain $$\begin{array}{cl} F & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\rho}w(x)s(x)dx} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{3}{62.4\left( {8 - \frac{8}{3}x} \right)x dx}} = 62.4{\int_{0}^{3}{\left( {8x - \frac{8}{3}x^{2}} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= 62.4\left. \left\lbrack {4x^{2} - \frac{8}{9}x^{3}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{3} = 748.8.} \end{array}$$ The water exerts a force of 748.8 lb on the end of the trough (step 4).

title: Chapter Opener: Finding Hydrostatic Force
snippet: Chapter Opener: Finding Hydrostatic Force: We now return our attention to the Hoover Dam, mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. The actual dam is arched, rather than flat, but we are going to make some simplifying assumptions to help...
body_xml: We now return our attention to the Hoover Dam, mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. The actual dam is arched, rather than flat, but we are going to make some simplifying assumptions to help us with the calculations. Assume the face of the Hoover Dam is shaped like an isosceles trapezoid with lower base $$750$$ ft, upper base $$1250$$ ft, and height $$750$$ ft (see the following figure). When the reservoir is full, Lake Mead’s maximum depth is about 530 ft, and the surface of the lake is about 10 ft below the top of the dam (see the following figure). Find the force on the face of the dam when the reservoir is full. The southwest United States has been experiencing a drought, and the surface of Lake Mead is about 125 ft below where it would be if the reservoir were full. What is the force on the face of the dam under these circumstances? We begin by establishing a frame of reference. As usual, we choose to orient the $$x \text{-axis}$$ vertically, with the downward direction being positive. This time, however, we are going to let $$x = 0$$ represent the top of the dam, rather than the surface of the water. When the reservoir is full, the surface of the water is $$10$$ ft below the top of the dam, so $$s(x) = x - 10$$ (see the following figure). Figure 2.60 We first choose a frame of reference. To find the width function, we again turn to similar triangles as shown in the figure below. Figure 2.61 We use similar triangles to determine a function for the width of the dam. (a) Assumed dimensions of the dam; (b) highlighting the similar triangles. From the figure, we see that $$w(x) = 750 + 2r.$$ Using properties of similar triangles, we get $$r = 250 - \left( {1/3} \right)x.$$ Thus, $$w(x) = 1250 - \frac{2}{3}x \text{(step 2).}$$ Using a weight-density of $$62.4$$ lb/ft3 (step 3) and applying Equation 2.13, we get $$\begin{array}{cl} F & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\rho}w(x)s(x)dx} \\ & {= {\int_{10}^{540}{62.4\left( {1250 - \frac{2}{3}x} \right)\left( {x - 10} \right)dx}} = 62.4{\int_{10}^{540}{- \frac{2}{3}\left\lbrack {x^{2} - 1885x + 18750} \right\rbrack}}dx} \\ & {= -62.4\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} - \frac{1885x^{2}}{2} + 18750x} \right\rbrack \right|_{10}^{540} \approx 8,832,245,000 \text{lb} = 4,416,122.5 \text{t} .} \end{array}$$ Note the change from pounds to tons $$(2000$$ lb = $$1$$ ton) (step 4). Notice that the drought changes our depth function, $$s(x),$$ and our limits of integration. We have $$s(x) = x - 135.$$ The lower limit of integration is $$135.$$ The upper limit remains $$540.$$ Evaluating the integral, we get $$\begin{array}{cl} F & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\rho}w(x)s(x)dx} \\ & {= {\int_{135}^{540}{62.4\left( {1250 - \frac{2}{3}x} \right)\left( {x - 135} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= -62.4\left( \frac{2}{3} \right){\int_{135}^{540}{\left( {x - 1875} \right)\left( {x - 135} \right)dx}} = -62.4\left( \frac{2}{3} \right){\int_{135}^{540}{\left( {x^{2} - 2010x + 253125} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= -62.4\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{3}}{3} - 1005x^{2} + 253125x} \right\rbrack \right|_{135}^{540} \approx 5,015,230,000 \text{lb} = 2,507,615 \text{t} .} \end{array}$$

<example number="2.29" title="Finding the Center of Mass of Objects along a Line">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose four point masses are placed on a number line as follows:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} {m_{1} = 30 \text{kg,} \text{placed at} x_{1} = -2 \text{m} } & & & {m_{2} = 5 \text{kg,} \text{placed at} x_{2} = 3 \text{m} } \\ {m_{3} = 10 \text{kg,} \text{placed at} x_{3} = 6 \text{m} } & & & {m_{4} = 15 \text{kg,} \text{placed at} x_{4} = -3 \text{m} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Find the moment of the system with respect to the origin and find the center of mass of the system.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we need to calculate the moment of the system:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} M & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{4}m_{i}}x_{i}} \\ & {= -60 + 15 + 60 - 45 = -30.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, to find the center of mass, we need the total mass of the system:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{4}m_{i}}} \\ & {= 30 + 5 + 10 + 15 = 60 \text{kg} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M}{m} = \frac{-30}{60} = - \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The center of mass is located 1/2 m to the left of the origin.</paragraph>
    </solution>

Then the moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}$$ of the system with respect to the x- and y-axes, respectively, are given by</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>First we calculate the total mass of the system:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$m = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{3}m_{i}} = 2 + 6 + 4 = 12 \text{kg} .$$</paragraph>

      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ {M_{y} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{3}m_{i}}x_{i} = -2 + 6 + 8 = 12,} \\ {M_{x} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{3}m_{i}}y_{i} = 6 + 6 - 8 = 4.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{12}{12} = 1 \text{and} \overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}.$$</paragraph>

body_xml: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ and below by the x-axis over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack.$$ Find the centroid of the region. The region is depicted in the following figure. Since we are only asked for the centroid of the region, rather than the mass or moments of the associated lamina, we know the density constant $$\rho$$ cancels out of the calculations eventually. Therefore, for the sake of convenience, let’s assume $$\rho = 1.$$ First, we need to calculate the total mass: $$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= \rho\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx = {\int_{0}^{4}\sqrt{x}} dx} \\ & {= \left. {\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}} \right|_{0}^{4} = \frac{2}{3}\left\lbrack {8 - 0} \right\rbrack = \frac{16}{3}.} \end{array}$$ Next, we compute the moments: $$\begin{array}{cl} M_{x} & {= \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}{2}dx}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\frac{x}{2}dx}} = \left. {\frac{1}{4}x^{2}} \right|_{0}^{4} = 4} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{array}{cl} M_{y} & {= \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{x}dx}} = {\int_{0}^{4}x^{3/2}}dx} \\ & {= \left. {\frac{2}{5}x^{5/2}} \right|_{0}^{4} = \frac{2}{5}\left\lbrack {32 - 0} \right\rbrack = \frac{64}{5}.} \end{array}$$ Thus, we have $$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{64/5}{16/3} = \frac{64}{5} \cdot \frac{3}{16} = \frac{12}{5} \text{and} \overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{4}{16/3} = 4 \cdot \frac{3}{16} = \frac{3}{4}.$$ The centroid of the region is $$\left( {{12/5},{3/4}} \right).$$

title: Center of Mass of a Lamina Bounded by Two Functions
snippet: Center of Mass of a Lamina Bounded by Two Functions: Center of Mass of a Lamina Bounded by Two Functions Let R denote a region bounded above by the graph of a continuous function f(x), below by the graph of the continuous function g(x),...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.13" title="Center of Mass of a Lamina Bounded by Two Functions">
    <heading level="4">Center of Mass of a Lamina Bounded by Two Functions</heading>
    <paragraph>Let R denote a region bounded above by the graph of a continuous function $$f(x),$$ below by the graph of the continuous function $$g(x),$$ and on the left and right by the lines $$x = a$$ and $$x = b,$$ respectively. Let $$\rho$$ denote the density of the associated lamina. Then we can make the following statements:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The mass of the lamina is $$m = \rho\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack dx.$$ (2.21)</item>
      <item>The moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}$$ of the lamina with respect to the x- and y-axes, respectively, are $$M_{x} = \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left( {\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2} - \left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right)}}dx \text{and} M_{y} = \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{x\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack dx}}.$$ (2.22)</item>
      <item>The coordinates of the center of mass $$\left( {\overset{-}{x},\overset{-}{y}} \right)$$ are $$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} \text{and} \overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m}.$$ (2.23)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Finding the Centroid of a Region Bounded by Two Functions
snippet: Finding the Centroid of a Region Bounded by Two Functions: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function f(x) = 1 - x^{2} and below by the graph of the function g(x) = x - 1. Find the centroid of the region. The region is...
body_xml: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function $$f(x) = 1 - x^{2}$$ and below by the graph of the function $$g(x) = x - 1.$$ Find the centroid of the region. The region is depicted in the following figure. The graphs of the functions intersect at $$\left( {-2,-3} \right)$$ and $$(1,0),$$ so we integrate from −2 to 1. Once again, for the sake of convenience, assume $$\rho = 1.$$ First, we need to calculate the total mass: $$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= \rho\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack dx} \\ & {= {\int_{-2}^{1}\left\lbrack {1 - x^{2} - (x - 1)} \right\rbrack}dx = \int_{-2}^{1}(2 - x^{2} - x)dx} \\ & {= \left. \left\lbrack {2x - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{-2}^{1} = \left\lbrack {2 - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {-4 + \frac{8}{3} - 2} \right\rbrack = \frac{9}{2}.} \end{array}$$ Next, we compute the moments: $$\begin{array}{cl} M_{x} & {= \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{1}{2}\left( {\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2} - \left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right)}}dx} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{-2}^{1}{\left( {\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)^{2} - \left( {x - 1} \right)^{2}} \right)dx}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{1}\left( {x^{4} - 3x^{2} + 2x} \right)dx} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - x^{3} + x^{2}} \right\rbrack \right|_{-2}^{1} = - \frac{27}{10}} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{matrix} M_{y} & {= \rho\int_{a}^{b}x\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack dx} \\ & {= \int_{-2}^{1}x\left\lbrack {\left( 1 - x^{2} \right) - (x - 1)} \right\rbrack dx = \int_{-2}^{1}x\left\lbrack 2 - x^{2} - x \right\rbrack dx} \\ {= \int_{-2}^{1}\left( 2x - x^{3} - x^{2} \right)dx} & \\ & {= \left. \left\lbrack x^{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4} - \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack \right|_{-2}^{1} = - \frac{9}{4}.} \end{matrix}$$ Therefore, we have $$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = - \frac{9}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{9} = - \frac{1}{2} \text{and} \overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = - \frac{27}{10} \cdot \frac{2}{9} = - \frac{3}{5}.$$ The centroid of the region is $$\left( {-\left( {1/2} \right),-\left( {3/5} \right)} \right).$$

title: Finding the Centroid of a Symmetric Region
snippet: Finding the Centroid of a Symmetric Region: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function f(x) = 4 - x^{2} and below by the x-axis. Find the centroid of the region. The region is depicted in the following figure. The...
body_xml: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function $$f(x) = 4 - x^{2}$$ and below by the x-axis. Find the centroid of the region. The region is depicted in the following figure. The region is symmetric with respect to the y-axis. Therefore, the x-coordinate of the centroid is zero. We need only calculate $$\overset{-}{y}.$$ Once again, for the sake of convenience, assume $$\rho = 1.$$ First, we calculate the total mass: $$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= \rho\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx} \\ & {= {\int_{-2}^{2}\left( {4 - x^{2}} \right)}dx} \\ & {= \left. \left\lbrack {4x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack \right|_{-2}^{2} = \frac{32}{3}.} \end{array}$$ Next, we calculate the moments. We only need $$M_{x}:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} M_{x} & {= \rho{\int_{a}^{b}{\frac{\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}{2}dx}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2}\left\lbrack {4 - x^{2}} \right\rbrack^{2}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-2}^{2}\left( {16 - 8x^{2} + x^{4}} \right)dx} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}\left. \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{8x^{3}}{3} + 16x} \right\rbrack \right|_{-2}^{2} = \frac{256}{15}.} \end{array}$$ Then we have $$\overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{256}{15} \cdot \frac{3}{32} = \frac{8}{5}.$$ The centroid of the region is $$\left( {0,{8/5}} \right).$$

snippet: Theorem of Pappus for Volume: Theorem of Pappus for Volume Let R be a region in the plane and let l be a line in the plane that does not intersect R. Then the volume of the solid of revolution formed by revolving R around l is equal to the...

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.14" title="Theorem of Pappus for Volume">
    <heading level="4">Theorem of Pappus for Volume</heading>
    <paragraph>Let R be a region in the plane and let l be a line in the plane that does not intersect R. Then the volume of the solid of revolution formed by revolving R around l is equal to the area of R multiplied by the distance d traveled by the centroid of R.</paragraph>

title: Using the Theorem of Pappus for Volume
snippet: Using the Theorem of Pappus for Volume: Let R be a circle of radius 2 centered at \left( {4,0} \right). Use the theorem of Pappus for volume to find the volume of the torus generated by revolving R around the y-axis. The region and torus...
body_xml: Let R be a circle of radius 2 centered at $$\left( {4,0} \right).$$ Use the theorem of Pappus for volume to find the volume of the torus generated by revolving R around the y-axis. The region and torus are depicted in the following figure. The region R is a circle of radius 2, so the area of R is $$A = 4\pi$$ units2. By the symmetry principle, the centroid of R is the center of the circle. The centroid travels around the y-axis in a circular path of radius 4, so the centroid travels $$d = 8\pi$$ units. Then, the volume of the torus is $$A \cdot d = 32\pi^{2}$$ units3.

    <solution>
      <paragraph>We need to apply the chain rule in both cases.</paragraph>

title: Properties of the Natural Logarithm
snippet: Properties of the Natural Logarithm: Properties of the Natural Logarithm If a,b > 0 and r is a rational number, then \ln 1 = 0 \ln \left( {ab} \right) = \ln a + \ln b \ln \left( \frac{a}{b} \right) = \ln a - \ln b \ln \left( a^{r} \right)...

    <heading level="4">Properties of the Natural Logarithm</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$a,b > 0$$ and $$r$$ is a rational number, then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\ln 1 = 0$$</item>
      <item>$$\ln \left( {ab} \right) = \ln a + \ln b$$</item>
      <item>$$\ln \left( \frac{a}{b} \right) = \ln a - \ln b$$</item>
      <item>$$\ln \left( a^{r} \right) = r \ln a$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Using Properties of Logarithms: Use properties of logarithms to simplify the following expression into a single logarithm: \ln 9 - 2 \ln 3 + \ln \left( \frac{1}{3} \right). We have \ln 9 - 2 \ln 3 + \ln \left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \ln...
body_xml:
<example number="2.37" title="Using Properties of Logarithms">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use properties of logarithms to simplify the following expression into a single logarithm:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\ln 9 - 2 \ln 3 + \ln \left( \frac{1}{3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\ln 9 - 2 \ln 3 + \ln \left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \ln \left( 3^{2} \right) - 2 \ln 3 + \ln \left( 3^{-1} \right) = 2 \ln 3 - 2 \ln 3 - \ln 3 = -\ln 3.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.42" title="Population Growth">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the population of bacteria described earlier. This population grows according to the function $$f(t) = 200e^{0.02t},$$ where t is measured in minutes. How many bacteria are present in the population after $$5$$ hours $$(300$$ minutes)? When does the population reach $$100,000$$ bacteria?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have $$f(t) = 200e^{0.02t}.$$ Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(300) = 200e^{0.02{(300)}} \approx 80,686.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There are $$80,686$$ bacteria in the population after $$5$$ hours.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find when the population reaches $$100,000$$ bacteria, we solve the equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 100,000 & = & {200e^{0.02t}} \\ 500 & = & e^{0.02t} \\ {\ln 500} & = & {0.02t} \\ t & = & {\frac{\ln 500}{0.02} \approx 310.73.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The population reaches $$100,000$$ bacteria after $$310.73$$ minutes.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.43" title="Compound Interest">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A 25-year-old student is offered an opportunity to invest some money in a retirement account that pays $$5\%$$ annual interest compounded continuously. How much does the student need to invest today to have $$\$1$$ million when she retires at age $$65?$$ What if she could earn $$6\%$$ annual interest compounded continuously instead?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 1,000,000 & = & {Pe^{0.05{(40)}}} \\ P & = & 135,335.28. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>She must invest $$\$135,335.28$$ at $$5\%$$ interest.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If, instead, she is able to earn $$6\%,$$ then the equation becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 1,000,000 & = & {Pe^{0.06{(40)}}} \\ P & = & 90,717.95. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In this case, she needs to invest only $$\$90,717.95.$$ This is roughly two-thirds the amount she needs to invest at $$5\%.$$ The fact that the interest is compounded continuously greatly magnifies the effect of the $$1\%$$ increase in interest rate.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Doubling Time
snippet: Using the Doubling Time: Assume a population of fish grows exponentially. A pond is stocked initially with 500 fish. After 6 months, there are 1000 fish in the pond. The owner will allow his friends and neighbors to fish on his pond after...
body_xml:
<example number="2.44" title="Using the Doubling Time">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Assume a population of fish grows exponentially. A pond is stocked initially with $$500$$ fish. After $$6$$ months, there are $$1000$$ fish in the pond. The owner will allow his friends and neighbors to fish on his pond after the fish population reaches $$10,000.$$ When will the owner’s friends be allowed to fish?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We know it takes the population of fish $$6$$ months to double in size. So, if t represents time in months, by the doubling-time formula, we have $$6 = {\left( {\ln 2} \right)/k}.$$ Then, $$k = {\left( {\ln 2} \right)/6}.$$ Thus, the population is given by $$y = 500e^{{({{({\ln 2})}/6})}t}.$$ To figure out when the population reaches $$10,000$$ fish, we must solve the following equation:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 10,000 & = & {500e^{(\ln 2/6)t}} \\ 20 & = & e^{(\ln 2/6)t} \\ {\ln 20} & = & {\left( \frac{\ln 2}{6} \right)t} \\ t & = & {\frac{6\left( {\ln 20} \right)}{\ln 2} \approx 25.93.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The owner’s friends have to wait $$25.93$$ months (a little more than $$2$$ years) to fish in the pond.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Newton’s Law of Cooling
snippet: Newton’s Law of Cooling: According to experienced baristas, the optimal temperature to serve coffee is between 155^\circ \text{F} and 175^\circ \text{F} . Suppose coffee is poured at a temperature of 200^\circ \text{F} , and after 2...
body_xml:
<example number="2.45" title="Newton’s Law of Cooling">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>According to experienced baristas, the optimal temperature to serve coffee is between $$155^\circ \text{F}$$ and $$175^\circ \text{F} .$$ Suppose coffee is poured at a temperature of $$200^\circ \text{F} ,$$ and after $$2$$ minutes in a $$70^\circ \text{F}$$ room it has cooled to $$180^\circ \text{F} .$$ When is the coffee first cool enough to serve? When is the coffee too cold to serve? Round answers to the nearest half minute.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} T & = & {\left( {T_{0} - T_{a}} \right)e^{-kt} + T_{a}} \\ 180 & = & {(200 - 70)e^{-k{(2)}} + 70} \\ 110 & = & {130e^{-2k}} \\ \frac{11}{13} & = & e^{-2k} \\ {\ln \frac{11}{13}} & = & {-2k} \\ {\ln 11 - \ln 13} & = & {-2k} \\ k & = & {\frac{\ln 13 - \ln 11}{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, the model is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$T = 130e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t} + 70.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coffee reaches $$175^\circ \text{F}$$ when</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 175 & = & {130e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t} + 70} \\ 105 & = & {130e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t}} \\ \frac{21}{26} & = & e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t} \\ {\ln \frac{21}{26}} & = & {\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2}t} \\ {\ln 21 - \ln 26} & = & {\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2}t} \\ t & = & {\frac{2\left( {\ln 21 - \ln 26} \right)}{\ln 11 - \ln 13} \approx 2.56.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coffee can be served about $$2.5$$ minutes after it is poured. The coffee reaches $$155^\circ \text{F}$$ at</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 155 & = & {130e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t} + 70} \\ 85 & = & {130e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t}} \\ \frac{17}{26} & = & e^{{(\frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2})}t} \\ {\ln 17 - \ln 26} & = & {\left( \frac{\ln 11 - \ln 13}{2} \right)t} \\ t & = & {\frac{2\left( {\ln 17 - \ln 26} \right)}{\ln 11 - \ln 13} \approx 5.09.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The coffee is too cold to be served about $$5$$ minutes after it is poured.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Radiocarbon Dating
snippet: Radiocarbon Dating: One of the most common applications of an exponential decay model is carbon dating. \text{Carbon-} 14 decays (emits a radioactive particle) at a regular and consistent exponential rate. Therefore, if we know how much...
body_xml:
<example number="2.46" title="Radiocarbon Dating">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>One of the most common applications of an exponential decay model is carbon dating. $$\text{Carbon-} 14$$ decays (emits a radioactive particle) at a regular and consistent exponential rate. Therefore, if we know how much carbon was originally present in an object and how much carbon remains, we can determine the age of the object. The half-life of $$\text{carbon-} 14$$ is approximately $$5730$$ years—meaning, after that many years, half the material has converted from the original $$\text{carbon-} 14$$ to the new nonradioactive $$\text{nitrogen-} 14.$$ If we have $$100$$ g $$\text{carbon-} 14$$ today, how much is left in $$50$$ years? If an artifact that originally contained $$100$$ g of carbon now contains $$10$$ g of carbon, how old is it? Round the answer to the nearest hundred years.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 5730 & = & \frac{\ln 2}{k} \\ k & = & {\frac{\ln 2}{5730}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the model says</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = 100e^{-{({\ln 2/5730})}t}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In $$50$$ years, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} y & = & {100e^{-{({\ln 2/5730})}{(50)}}} \\ & \approx & {99.40.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, in $$50$$ years, $$99.40$$ g of $$\text{carbon-} 14$$ remains.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To determine the age of the artifact, we must solve</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 10 & = & {100e^{-{({\ln 2/5730})}t}} \\ \frac{1}{10} & = & e^{-{({\ln 2/5730})}t} \\ t & \approx & 19035. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The artifact is about $$19,000$$ years old.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.48" title="Integrals Involving Hyperbolic Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate the following integrals:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$${\int{x \cosh \left( x^{2} \right)d}}x$$</item>
        <item>$${\int{\tanh x d}}x$$</item>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can use u-substitution in both cases.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$u = x^{2}.$$ Then, $$du = 2x dx$$ and $${\int{x \cosh \left( x^{2} \right)d}}x = {\int\frac{1}{2}}\cosh u du = \frac{1}{2}\sinh u + C = \frac{1}{2}\sinh \left( x^{2} \right) + C.$$</item>
        <item>Let $$u = \cosh x.$$ Then, $$du = \sinh x dx$$ and $${\int{\tanh x d}}x = {\int{\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}d}}x = {\int{\frac{1}{u}d}}u = \ln |u| + C = \ln \left| {\cosh x} \right| + C.$$ Note that $$\cosh x > 0$$ for all $$x,$$ so we can eliminate the absolute value signs and obtain $${\int{\tanh x d}}x = \ln \left( {\cosh x} \right) + C.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using a Catenary to Find the Length of a Cable
snippet: Using a Catenary to Find the Length of a Cable: Assume a hanging cable has the shape 10 \cosh \left( {x/10} \right) for -15 \leq x \leq 15, where x is measured in feet. Determine the length of the cable (in feet). Recall from Section 2.4...
body_xml:
<example number="2.51" title="Using a Catenary to Find the Length of a Cable">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Assume a hanging cable has the shape $$10 \cosh \left( {x/10} \right)$$ for $$-15 \leq x \leq 15,$$ where $$x$$ is measured in feet. Determine the length of the cable (in feet).</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Recall from Section $$2.4$$ that the formula for arc length is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Arc Length} = {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We have $$f(x) = 10 \cosh \left( {x/10} \right),$$ so $$f^{\prime}(x) = \sinh \left( {x/10} \right).$$ Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Arc Length} & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} dx} \\ & {= {\int_{-15}^{15}\sqrt{1 + \sinh^{2}\left( \frac{x}{10} \right)}} dx.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now recall that $$1 + \sinh^{2}x = \cosh^{2}x,$$ so we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{Arc Length} & {= {\int_{-15}^{15}\sqrt{1 + \sinh^{2}\left( \frac{x}{10} \right)}} dx} \\ & {= \int_{-15}^{15}\cosh \left( \frac{x}{10} \right)dx} \\ & {= 10 \sinh \left. \left( \frac{x}{10} \right) \right|_{-15}^{15} = 10\left\lbrack {\sinh \left( \frac{3}{2} \right) - \sinh \left( {- \frac{3}{2}} \right)} \right\rbrack = 20 \sinh \left( \frac{3}{2} \right)} \\ & {\approx 42.586 \text{ft} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Integration by Parts
snippet: Using Integration by Parts: Use integration by parts with u = x and dv = \sin x dx to evaluate \int{x\sin x dx.} By choosing u = x, we have du = 1dx. Since dv = \sin x dx, we get v = {\int{\sin x dx = -\cos x.}} It is handy to keep track...
body_xml:
<example number="3.1" title="Using Integration by Parts">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use integration by parts with $$u = x$$ and $$dv = \sin x dx$$ to evaluate $$\int{x\sin x dx.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>By choosing $$u = x,$$ we have $$du = 1dx.$$ Since $$dv = \sin x dx,$$ we get $$v = {\int{\sin x dx = -\cos x.}}$$ It is handy to keep track of these values as follows:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcrll} u & = & x & & {dv} & = & {\sin x dx} \\ {du} & = & {1dx} & & v & = & {\int{\sin x dx = -\cos x.}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Applying the integration-by-parts formula results in</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clcl} {\int{x\sin x dx}} & {= (x)(-\cos x) - {\int{(-\cos x)(1dx)}}} & & { \text{Substitute} .} \\ & {= -x\cos x + {\int{\cos x dx}}} & & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & {= -x\cos x + \sin x + C.} & & { \text{Use} {\int{\cos x dx = \sin x + C.}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>At this point, there are probably a few items that need clarification. First of all, you may be curious about what would have happened if we had chosen $$u = \sin x$$ and $$dv = x.$$ If we had done so, then we would have $$du = \cos x{dx}$$ and $$v = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}.$$ Thus, after applying integration by parts, we have $$\int^{}x\sin x dx = \frac{1}{2}x^{2}\sin x - \int^{}\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\cos x dx.$$ Unfortunately, with the new integral, we are in no better position than before. It is important to keep in mind that when we apply integration by parts, we may need to try several choices for $$u$$ and $$dv$$ before finding a choice that works.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Second, you may wonder why, when we find $$v = \int^{}\sin x dx = -\cos x,$$ we do not use $$v = -\cos x + K.$$ To see that it makes no difference, we can rework the problem using $$v = -\cos x + K:$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\int^{ }x\sin x dx} & {= (x)(-\cos x + K) - \int^{ }(-\cos x + K)(1dx)} \\ & {= -x\cos x + Kx + \int^{ }\cos x dx - \int^{ }Kdx} \\ & {= -x\cos x + Kx + \sin x - Kx + C} \\ & {= -x\cos x + \sin x + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>As you can see, it makes no difference in the final solution.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Last, we can check to make sure that our antiderivative is correct by differentiating $$-x\cos x + \sin x + C:$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( {-x\cos x + \sin x + C} \right)} & {= (-1)\cos x + (-x)(-\sin x) + \cos x} \\ & {= x\sin x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, the antiderivative checks out.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Using Integration by Parts
snippet: Using Integration by Parts: Evaluate \int{\frac{\ln x}{x^{3}}dx.} Begin by rewriting the integral: {\int{\frac{\ln x}{x^{3}}dx}} = \int^{}x^{-3}\ln x dx. Since this integral contains the algebraic function x^{-3} and the logarithmic...
body_xml:
<example number="3.2" title="Using Integration by Parts">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int{\frac{\ln x}{x^{3}}dx.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by rewriting the integral:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int{\frac{\ln x}{x^{3}}dx}} = \int^{}x^{-3}\ln x dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since this integral contains the algebraic function $$x^{-3}$$ and the logarithmic function $$\ln x,$$ choose $$u = \ln x,$$ since L comes before A in LIATE. After we have chosen $$u = \ln x,$$ we must choose $$dv = x^{-3}dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, since $$u = \ln x,$$ we have $$du = \frac{1}{x}dx.$$ Also, $$v = \int^{}x^{-3}dx = - \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}.$$ Summarizing,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcrll} u & = & {\ln x} & & {dv} & = & {x^{-3}dx} \\ {du} & = & {\frac{1}{x}dx} & & v & = & {\int^{}x^{-3}dx = - \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting into the integration-by-parts formula (Equation 3.1) gives</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\int{\frac{\ln x}{x^{3}}dx}} & {= \int^{}x^{-3}\ln x dx = \left( {\ln x)(- \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}} \right) - \int^{}\left( {- \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}} \right)(\frac{1}{x}dx)} & & & \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}\ln x + \int^{}\frac{1}{2}x^{-3}dx} & & & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2}x^{-2}\ln x - \frac{1}{4}x^{-2} + C} & & & { \text{Integrate} .} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{2x^{2}}\ln x - \frac{1}{4x^{2}} + C.} & & & \text{Rewrite with positive integers.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once
snippet: Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once: Evaluate \int^{}x^{2}e^{3x}dx. Using LIATE, choose u = x^{2} and dv = e^{3x}dx. Thus, du = 2x dx and v = {\int{e^{3x}dx = \left( \frac{1}{3} \right)e^{3x}}}. Therefore, \begin{array}{rllcrll} u...
body_xml:
<example number="3.3" title="Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int^{}x^{2}e^{3x}dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using LIATE, choose $$u = x^{2}$$ and $$dv = e^{3x}dx.$$ Thus, $$du = 2x dx$$ and $$v = {\int{e^{3x}dx = \left( \frac{1}{3} \right)e^{3x}}}.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcrll} u & = & x^{2} & & {dv} & = & {e^{3x}dx} \\ {du} & = & {2x dx} & & v & = & {{\int{e^{3x}dx = \frac{1}{3}e^{3x}}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting into Equation 3.1 produces</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int{x^{2}e^{3x}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}x^{2}e^{3x} - {\int{\frac{2}{3}xe^{3x}dx}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We still cannot integrate $$\int{\frac{2}{3}xe^{3x}dx}$$ directly, but the integral now has a lower power on $$x.$$ We can evaluate this new integral by using integration by parts again. To do this, choose $$u = x$$ and $$dv = \frac{2}{3}e^{3x}dx.$$ Thus, $$du = dx$$ and $$v = {\int{\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)e^{3x}dx = \left( \frac{2}{9} \right)e^{3x}}}.$$ Now we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcrll} u & = & x & & {dv} & = & {\frac{2}{3}e^{3x}dx} \\ {du} & = & {dx} & & v & = & {{\int{\frac{2}{3}e^{3x}dx = \frac{2}{9}e^{3x}}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting back into the previous equation yields</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}x^{2}e^{3x}dx = \frac{1}{3}x^{2}e^{3x} - \left( {\frac{2}{9}xe^{3x} - \int^{}\frac{2}{9}e^{3x}dx} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After evaluating the last integral and simplifying, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int{x^{2}e^{3x}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}x^{2}e^{3x} - \frac{2}{9}xe^{3x} + \frac{2}{27}e^{3x} + C.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying Integration by Parts When LIATE Doesn’t Quite Work
snippet: Applying Integration by Parts When LIATE Doesn’t Quite Work: Evaluate \int^{}t^{3}e^{t^{2}}dt. If we use a strict interpretation of the mnemonic LIATE to make our choice of u, we end up with u = t^{3} and dv = e^{t^{2}}dt. Unfortunately,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.4" title="Applying Integration by Parts When LIATE Doesn’t Quite Work">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int^{}t^{3}e^{t^{2}}dt.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>If we use a strict interpretation of the mnemonic LIATE to make our choice of $$u,$$ we end up with $$u = t^{3}$$ and $$dv = e^{t^{2}}dt.$$ Unfortunately, this choice won’t work because we are unable to evaluate $$\int^{}e^{t^{2}}dt.$$ However, since we can evaluate $$\int^{}te^{t^{2}}dt,$$ we can try choosing $$u = t^{2}$$ and $$dv = te^{t^{2}}dt.$$ With these choices we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rllcrll} u & = & t^{2} & & {dv} & = & {te^{t^{2}}dt} \\ {du} & = & {2t dt} & & v & = & {\int^{}te^{t^{2}}dt = \frac{1}{2}e^{t^{2}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\int^{ }t^{3}e^{t^{2}}dt} & {= \frac{1}{2}t^{2}e^{t^{2}} - {\int{\frac{1}{2}e^{t^{2}}2tdt}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}t^{2}e^{t^{2}} - \frac{1}{2}e^{t^{2}} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once
snippet: Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once: Evaluate \int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx. This integral appears to have only one function—namely, \sin (\ln x) —however, we can always use the constant function 1 as the other function. In this example,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.5" title="Applying Integration by Parts More Than Once">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This integral appears to have only one function—namely, $$\sin (\ln x)$$ —however, we can always use the constant function 1 as the other function. In this example, let’s choose $$u = \sin (\ln x)$$ and $$dv = 1dx.$$ (The decision to use $$u = \sin (\ln x)$$ is easy. We can’t choose $$dv = \sin (\ln x)dx$$ because if we could integrate it, we wouldn’t be using integration by parts in the first place!) Consequently, $$du = (1/x)\cos (\ln x)dx$$ and $$v = \int^{}1dx = x.$$ After applying integration by parts to the integral and simplifying, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx = x\sin \left( {\ln x} \right) - \int^{}\cos \left( {\ln x} \right)dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Unfortunately, this process leaves us with a new integral that is very similar to the original. However, let’s see what happens when we apply integration by parts again. This time let’s choose $$u = \cos (\ln x)$$ and $$dv = 1dx,$$ making $$du = -(1/x)\sin (\ln x)dx$$ and $$v = \int^{}1dx = x.$$ Substituting, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx = x\sin \left( {\ln x} \right) - \left( {x\cos (\ln x)-\int^{} - \sin (\ln x)dx} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After simplifying, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx = x\sin (\ln x) - x\cos (\ln x) - \int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The last integral is now the same as the original. It may seem that we have simply gone in a circle, but now we can actually evaluate the integral. To see how to do this more clearly, substitute $$I = \int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx.$$ Thus, the equation becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$I = x\sin (\ln x) - x\cos (\ln x) - I.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First, add $$I$$ to both sides of the equation to obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$2I = x\sin (\ln x) - x\cos (\ln x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, divide by 2:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$I = \frac{1}{2}x\sin (\ln x) - \frac{1}{2}x\cos (\ln x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substituting $$I = \int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx$$ again, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx = \frac{1}{2}x\sin (\ln x) - \frac{1}{2}x\cos (\ln x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>From this we see that $$(1/2)x\sin (\ln x) - (1/2)x\cos (\ln x)$$ is an antiderivative of $$\sin (\ln x)dx.$$ For the most general antiderivative, add $$+ C:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int^{}\sin (\ln x)dx = \frac{1}{2}x\sin (\ln x) - \frac{1}{2}x\cos (\ln x) + C.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>If this method feels a little strange at first, we can check the answer by differentiation:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\frac{1}{2}x\sin (\ln x) - \frac{1}{2}x\cos (\ln x)} \right)} \\ \\ {= \frac{1}{2}(\sin (\ln x)) + \cos (\ln x) \cdot \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{2}x - \left( {\frac{1}{2}\cos (\ln x) - \sin (\ln x) \cdot \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{2}x} \right)} \\ {= \sin (\ln x).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Finding the Area of a Region
snippet: Finding the Area of a Region: Find the area of the region bounded above by the graph of y = \tan^{-1}x and below by the x -axis over the interval \left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack. This region is shown in Figure 3.2. To find the area, we...
body_xml: Find the area of the region bounded above by the graph of $$y = \tan^{-1}x$$ and below by the $$x$$ -axis over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ This region is shown in Figure 3.2. To find the area, we must evaluate $$\int\limits_{0}^{1}\tan^{-1}x dx.$$ For this integral, let’s choose $$u = \tan^{-1}x$$ and $$dv = dx,$$ thereby making $$du = \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}dx$$ and $$v = x.$$ After applying the integration-by-parts formula (Equation 3.2) we obtain $${ \text{Area} = x\tan^{-1}\left. x \right|_{0}^{1}} - {\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\frac{x}{x^{2} + 1}dx.}}$$ Use u-substitution to obtain $$\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\frac{x}{x^{2} + 1}dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln \left| x^{2} + 1|_{0}^{1}. \right.}$$ Thus, $$\left. \text{Area} = x \tan^{- 1}x|_{0}^{1} - \frac{1}{2}\ln\left| x^{2} \right. + 1 \middle| |_{0}^{1} = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\ln 2. \right.$$ At this point it might not be a bad idea to do a “reality check” on the reasonableness of our solution. Since $$\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\ln 2 \approx 0.4388,$$ and from Figure 3.2 we expect our area to be slightly less than 0.5, this solution appears to be reasonable.

title: Finding a Volume of Revolution
snippet: Finding a Volume of Revolution: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the graph of f(x) = e^{-x}, the x-axis, the y-axis, and the line x = 1 about the y-axis. The best option to solving this problem is to...
body_xml: Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the graph of $$f(x) = e^{-x},$$ the x-axis, the y-axis, and the line $$x = 1$$ about the y-axis. The best option to solving this problem is to use the shell method. Begin by sketching the region to be revolved, along with a typical rectangle (see the following graph). To find the volume using shells, we must evaluate $$2\pi{\int_{0}^{1}{xe^{-x}dx}}.$$ To do this, let $$u = x$$ and $$dv = e^{-x}.$$ These choices lead to $$du = dx$$ and $$v = \int^{}e^{-x} = -e^{-x}.$$ Substituting into Equation 3.2, we obtain $$\begin{array}{clcl} \text{Volume} & {= 2\pi\int\limits_{0}^{1}xe^{-x}dx = 2\pi(-xe^{-x}|_{0}^{1} + \int\limits_{0}^{1}e^{-x}dx)} & & { \text{Use integration by parts} .} \\ & {{= -2\pi xe^{-x}|_{0}^{1}} - 2\pi e^{-x}|_{0}^{1}} & & {{ \text{Evaluate} \int\limits_{0}^{1}e^{-x}dx = -e^{-x}|_{0}^{1}}.} \\ & {= 2\pi - \frac{4\pi}{e}.} & & { \text{Evaluate and simplify} .} \end{array}$$ Again, it is a good idea to check the reasonableness of our solution. We observe that the solid has a volume slightly less than that of a cylinder of radius $$1$$ and height of $$1/e$$ added to the volume of a cone of base radius $$1$$ and height of $$1 - \frac{1}{e}.$$ Consequently, the solid should have a volume a bit less than $$\pi{(1)}^{2}\frac{1}{e} + \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)(1)^{2}\left( {1 - \frac{1}{e}} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3e} + \frac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.8177.$$ Since $$2\pi - \frac{4\pi}{e} \approx 1.6603,$$ we see that our calculated volume is reasonable.

<example number="3.9">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int\cos^{2}x\sin^{3}x dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To convert this integral to integrals of the form $$\int\cos^{j}x\sin x dx,$$ rewrite $$\sin^{3}x = \sin^{2}x\sin x$$ and make the substitution $$\sin^{2}x = 1 - \cos^{2}x.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {\int\cos^{2}x\sin^{3}x dx} & {= \int\cos^{2}x\left( 1 - \cos^{2}x \right)\sin x dx} & { \text{Let} u = \cos x; \text{then} du = -\sin x dx.} \\ & {= -\int u^{2}\left( 1 - u^{2} \right)du} & \\ & {= \int\left( u^{4} - u^{2} \right)du} & \\ & {= \frac{1}{5}u^{5} - \frac{1}{3}u^{3} + C} & \\ & {= \frac{1}{5}\cos^{5}x - \frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x + C.} & \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Problem-Solving Strategy
snippet: Problem-Solving Strategy: Integrating Products and Powers of sin x and cos x To integrate \int\cos^{j}x\sin^{k}x dx use the following strategies: If k is odd, rewrite \sin^{k}x = \sin^{k - 1}x\sin x and use the identity \sin^{2}x = 1 -...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Integrating Products and Powers of sin x and cos x</heading>
    <paragraph>To integrate $$\int\cos^{j}x\sin^{k}x dx$$ use the following strategies:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If $$k$$ is odd, rewrite $$\sin^{k}x = \sin^{k - 1}x\sin x$$ and use the identity $$\sin^{2}x = 1 - \cos^{2}x$$ to rewrite $$\sin^{k - 1}x$$ in terms of $$\cos x.$$ Integrate using the substitution $$u = \cos x.$$ This substitution makes $$du = -\sin x dx.$$</item>
      <item>If $$j$$ is odd, rewrite $$\cos^{j}x = \cos^{j - 1}x\cos x$$ and use the identity $$\cos^{2}x = 1 - \sin^{2}x$$ to rewrite $$\cos^{j - 1}x$$ in terms of $$\sin x.$$ Integrate using the substitution $$u = \sin x.$$ This substitution makes $$du = \cos x dx.$$ (Note: If both $$j$$ and $$k$$ are odd, either strategy 1 or strategy 2 may be used.)</item>
      <item>If both $$j$$ and $$k$$ are even, use $$\sin^{2}x = (1/2) - (1/2)\cos (2x)$$ and $$\cos^{2}x = (1/2) + (1/2)\cos (2x).$$ After applying these formulas, simplify and reapply strategies 1 through 3 as appropriate.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="3.11" title="Integrating ∫cosjxsinkxdx∫cosjxsinkxdx where k is Odd">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int\cos^{8}x\sin^{5}x dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the power on $$\sin x$$ is odd, use strategy 1. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clcl} {\int\cos^{8}x\sin^{5}x dx} & {= \int\cos^{8}x\sin^{4}x\sin x dx} & & { \text{Break off} \sin x.} \\ & {= \int\cos^{8}x{(\sin^{2}x)}^{2}\sin x dx} & & { \text{Rewrite} \sin^{4}x = {(\sin^{2}x)}^{2}.} \\ & {= \int\cos^{8}x{(1 - \cos^{2}x)}^{2}\sin x dx} & & { \text{Substitute} \sin^{2}x = 1 - \cos^{2}x.} \\ & {= \int u^{8}{(1 - u^{2})}^{2}(-du)} & & { \text{Let} u = \cos x \text{and} du = -\sin x dx.} \\ & {= \int\left( {-u^{8} + 2u^{10} - u^{12}} \right)du} & & { \text{Expand} .} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{9}u^{9} + \frac{2}{11}u^{11} - \frac{1}{13}u^{13} + C} & & { \text{Evaluate the integral} .} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{9}\cos^{9}x + \frac{2}{11}\cos^{11}x - \frac{1}{13}\cos^{13}x + C.} & & { \text{Substitute} u = \cos x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Integrating ∫cosjxsinkxdx∫cosjxsinkxdx where k and j are Even
snippet: Integrating ∫cosjxsinkxdx∫cosjxsinkxdx where k and j are Even: Evaluate \int\sin^{4}x dx. Since the power on \sin x is even \left( {k = 4} \right) and the power on \cos x is even \left( {j = 0} \right), we must use strategy 3. Thus,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.12" title="Integrating ∫cosjxsinkxdx∫cosjxsinkxdx where k and j are Even">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int\sin^{4}x dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the power on $$\sin x$$ is even $$\left( {k = 4} \right)$$ and the power on $$\cos x$$ is even $$\left( {j = 0} \right),$$ we must use strategy 3. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clcc} {\int\sin^{4}x dx} & {= \int\left( {\sin^{2}x} \right)^{2}dx} & & { \text{Rewrite} \sin^{4}x = \left( {\sin^{2}x} \right)^{2}.} \\ & {= \int\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos (2x)} \right)^{2}dx} & & { \text{Substitute} \sin^{2}x = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos (2x).} \\ & {= \int\left( {\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos \left( {2x} \right) + \frac{1}{4}\cos^{2}(2x)} \right)dx} & & { \text{Expand} \left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos (2x)} \right)^{2}.} \\ & {= \int\left( {\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos \left( {2x} \right) + \frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos (4x)} \right)dx.} & & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$\cos^{2}(2x)$$ has an even power, substitute $$\cos^{2}(2x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos \left( {4x} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {= \int\left( {\frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\cos \left( {2x} \right) + \frac{1}{8}\cos (4x)} \right)dx} & { \text{Simplify} .} \\ {= \frac{3}{8}x - \frac{1}{4}\sin \left( {2x} \right) + \frac{1}{32}\sin \left( {4x} \right) + C} & { \text{Evaluate the integral} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Problem-Solving Strategy: Integrating \int\tan^{k}x\sec^{j}x dx To integrate \int\tan^{k}x\sec^{j}x dx, use the following strategies: If j is even and j \geq 2, rewrite \sec^{j}x = \sec^{j - 2}x\sec^{2}x and use \sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x + 1...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Integrating $$\int\tan^{k}x\sec^{j}x dx$$</heading>
    <paragraph>To integrate $$\int\tan^{k}x\sec^{j}x dx,$$ use the following strategies:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If $$j$$ is even and $$j \geq 2,$$ rewrite $$\sec^{j}x = \sec^{j - 2}x\sec^{2}x$$ and use $$\sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x + 1$$ to rewrite $$\sec^{j - 2}x$$ in terms of $$\tan x.$$ Let $$u = \tan x$$ and $$du = \sec^{2}x{dx}.$$</item>
      <item>If $$k$$ is odd and $$j \geq 1,$$ rewrite $$\tan^{k}x\sec^{j}x = \tan^{k - 1}x\sec^{j - 1}x\sec x\tan x$$ and use $$\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1$$ to rewrite $$\tan^{k - 1}x$$ in terms of $$\sec x.$$ Let $$u = \sec x$$ and $$du = \sec x\tan x dx.$$ (Note: If $$j$$ is even and $$k$$ is odd, then either strategy 1 or strategy 2 may be used.)</item>
      <item>If $$k$$ is odd where $$k \geq 3$$ and $$j = 0,$$ rewrite $$\tan^{k}x = \tan^{k - 2}x\tan^{2}x = \tan^{k - 2}x(\sec^{2}x - 1) = \tan^{k - 2}x\sec^{2}x - \tan^{k - 2}x.$$ It may be necessary to repeat this process on the $$\tan^{k - 2}x$$ term.</item>
      <item>If $$k$$ is even and $$j$$ is odd, then use $$\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1$$ to express $$\tan^{k}x$$ in terms of $$\sec x.$$ Use integration by parts to integrate odd powers of $$\sec x.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the power on $$\sec x$$ is even, rewrite $$\sec^{4}x = \sec^{2}x\sec^{2}x$$ and use $$\sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x + 1$$ to rewrite the first $$\sec^{2}x$$ in terms of $$\tan x.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clcl} {\int\tan^{6}x\sec^{4}x dx} & {= \int\tan^{6}x\left( {\tan^{2}x + 1} \right)\sec^{2}x dx} & & { \text{Let} u = \tan x \text{and} du = \sec^{2}x{dx}.} \\ & {= \int u^{6}\left( {u^{2} + 1} \right)du} & & { \text{Expand} .} \\ & {= \int(u^{8} + u^{6})du} & & { \text{Evaluate the integral} .} \\ & {= \frac{1}{9}u^{9} + \frac{1}{7}u^{7} + C} & & { \text{Substitute} \tan x = u.} \\ & {= \frac{1}{9}\tan^{9}x + \frac{1}{7}\tan^{7}x + C.} & & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.16" title="Integrating ∫tankxsecjxdx∫tankxsecjxdx when kk is Odd">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int\tan^{5}x\sec^{3}x dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the power on $$\tan x$$ is odd, begin by rewriting $$\tan^{5}x\sec^{3}x = \tan^{4}x\sec^{2}x\sec x\tan x.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cllccc} {\tan^{5}x\sec^{3}x} & = & {\tan^{4}x\sec^{2}x\sec x\tan x.} & & & { \text{Write} \tan^{4}x = {(\tan^{2}x)}^{2}.} \\ {\int\tan^{5}x\sec^{3}x dx} & = & {\int{(\tan^{2}x)}^{2}\sec^{2}x\sec x\tan x dx} & & & { \text{Use} \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1.} \\ & = & {\int{(\sec^{2}x - 1)}^{2}\sec^{2}x\sec x\tan x dx} & & & { \text{Let} u = \sec x \text{and} du = \sec x\tan x dx.} \\ & = & {\int{(u^{2} - 1)}^{2}u^{2}du} & & & { \text{Expand} .} \\ & = & {\int\left( {u^{6} - 2u^{4} + u^{2}} \right)du} & & & { \text{Integrate} .} \\ & = & {\frac{1}{7}u^{7} - \frac{2}{5}u^{5} + \frac{1}{3}u^{3} + C} & & & { \text{Substitute} \sec x = u.} \\ & = & {\frac{1}{7}\sec^{7}x - \frac{2}{5}\sec^{5}x + \frac{1}{3}\sec^{3}x + C.} & & & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.17" title="Integrating ∫tankxdx∫tankxdx where kk is Odd and k≥3k≥3">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int\tan^{3}x dx.$$</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by rewriting $$\tan^{3}x = \tan x\tan^{2}x = \tan x\left( {\sec^{2}x - 1} \right) = \tan x\sec^{2}x - \tan x.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
